**Demand forecasting is not the same as predicting recorded sales.** If a store sells its last three units before noon, observed sales are three even if ten customers wanted the item. Stockouts censor demand. A model trained naively on those sales can predict low demand, order too little, and perpetuate the shortage.

**Build the data panel carefully.** For each store–item–time period, record sales, availability, prices, promotions, holidays, and lead times as they were known at the forecast origin. Future realized promotion effects or later inventory corrections must not leak into historical training features.

Use simple seasonal/intermittent-demand baselines before more complex global models. A global model shares patterns across related items, helping sparse series, but must still handle new products and retirements. Promotion effects can shift demand between substitutes rather than creating independent increases for every item. [3](https://otexts.com/fpp3/)

**Forecast uncertainty supports replenishment.** Inventory decisions need more than a mean: understock and overstock have different costs, and delivery lead time is uncertain. Quantiles or predictive distributions can support service-level decisions. Reconciliation can make store/region totals coherent, but coherence alone does not guarantee accuracy.

Evaluate with rolling forecast origins across seasons and lifecycle stages, then simulate inventory outcomes under realistic policies. MAPE is unsuitable for zero-demand periods. Report tail-item performance and stockout-related errors separately from aggregate volume-weighted metrics, which can look strong while niche items are chronically unavailable.

**Technical details and references.**

Build a store-SKU-time panel with stock availability, prices, promotions, calendars, and lead times recorded as known at forecast time. Observed sales during stockouts are censored demand, not true zero demand. Separate demand forecasting from inventory optimization, which additionally needs service levels, lead-time uncertainty, and holding/stockout costs.

Use global models to share information across related series, with intermittent-demand baselines for sparse items and calibrated quantiles for replenishment. Hierarchical reconciliation can make SKU/store/region totals coherent; bottom-up aggregation and forecast reconciliation have different error and computational tradeoffs. Promotion effects need cross-item substitution/cannibalization features rather than independent uplift per SKU.

Evaluate rolling-origin forecasts across seasons and product lifecycle stages. Use scaled/weighted error plus quantile coverage and inventory simulations; MAPE fails on zeros. Track availability of future covariates and prevent realized promotion outcomes from entering past forecasts. Provide cold-start category/content baselines and explicit retirement logic. Monitor aggregate accuracy and sparse-tail behavior separately, because pooled metrics can conceal chronic understocking of niche items.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Forecast demand quantiles for inventory decisions and reconcile aggregate forecasts using a hierarchy matrix when coherence is required. Evaluate rolling origins under lead-time constraints. Sales equal demand only when supply is available; stockouts censor observations, so naive training can interpret unmet demand as low interest and perpetuate understocking. [3](https://otexts.com/fpp3/)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://www.uber.com/blog/forecasting-introduction/) and [2](https://otexts.com/fpp3/hierarchical.html).
